idiom_name: hash of procs keyed by token type (nud/led) + binding power
implementation_notes: Ruby's hash-of-procs is the local idiom: each token type maps to a small rule carrying a binding power plus nud/led lambdas, and the loop stays a handful of lines because procs close over the parser. Ruby itself does not parse expressions for you either - Ripper exposes the bison-generated Ruby parser as events, tokens and S-expressions (it is what you use to analyse Ruby source), while a hand-written table is what you write for your own DSL; Ruby's own operator precedence is fixed by the language and is not negotiable at runtime. Choose the table when you want precise positions, custom AST shapes and control over errors; choose Racc, Parslet or ANTLR when the grammar is larger than its expression layer.
code_sketch:
RULES = Hash.new { |h, k| h[k] = { lbp: 0, nud: nil, led: nil } }
RULES[:minus] = { lbp: 30,
  nud: ->(p, _t)     { Neg.new(p.expr(70)) },
  led: ->(p, left, _t) { Sub.new(left, p.expr(31)) } }   # left-assoc: lbp + 1
def expr(min_bp)
  left = RULES[take.type][:nud]&.call(self, previous) or raise ParseError, "unexpected token"
  while min_bp < RULES[peek.type][:lbp]
    left = RULES[take.type][:led].call(self, left, previous)
  end
  left
end
pitfalls: Hash.new with a block mutates the table on every read: looking up an unknown token silently inserts a rule with lbp 0 instead of failing, and the block also runs for legitimate misses; use a frozen table plus fetch.
Ruby does not optimise tail calls by default and has a hard stack limit: deep expression nesting raises SystemStackError, so bound the depth before the VM does.
Procs are not checked against the call convention - an led lambda written with two parameters fails with ArgumentError at the first infix token, pointing into the loop rather than at the rule table.
